system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-08-03 15:20:00 to 2177-08-09 12:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis complicated by cirrhosis was admitted with recurrent cholangitis, presenting with fever and right upper quadrant pain. She had recently completed a course of ciprofloxacin but developed symptoms consistent with a flare. Imaging confirmed a persistent 7mm stone in the right intrahepatic duct, which could not be removed due to anatomical constraints. She was treated with intravenous meropenem, transitioned to ertapenem via a newly placed PICC line for a 14-day course, and showed clinical and laboratory improvement. Chronic medications were managed, with lisinopril and furosemide held initially and restarted at discharge. She was discharged home with home health support for IV antibiotics and plans for outpatient MRCP and gastroenterology follow-up.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  LIVER OR GALLBLADDER US (SINGLE ORGAN)

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with PSC and fever/RUQ pain // eval for stone,
duct dilation

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the abdomen were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS: 

LIVER: The echogenicity of the liver is homogeneous. The contour of the liver
is smooth. There is no focal liver mass. Main portal vein is patent with
hepatopetal flow. There is no ascites.

BILE DUCTS: There is no intrahepatic biliary dilation. The CBD measures 7 mm
and appears slightly thickened consistent with the provided diagnosis of
primary sclerosing cholangitis. No stones are visualized within the common
bile duct. As per the prior ultrasound report a retained stone measuring 1.3
cm is seen within the central intrahepatic ducts possibly within the trunk of
the right hepatic duct. There is no upstream intrahepatic biliary duct
dilation.

GALLBLADDER: Surgically absent.

PANCREAS: Head, body and tail of the pancreas are within normal limits,
without masses or pancreatic ductal dilatation.

RETROPERITONEUM: Visualized portions of aorta and IVC are within normal
limits.

IMPRESSION: 

As per the prior report there is retained stone in the central intrahepatic
ducts, possibly located in the trunk of the right hepatic duct. There is no
upstream intrahepatic biliary dilation. No stones are identified within the
common bile duct.

NOTIFICATION:  Findings were placed on the Dashboard by ___ at 17:03 on ___.

EXAMINATION:  MRCP

INDICATION:  PSC and chronic recurrent cholangitis, planning for possible
ERCP.  Assess biliary system for stones, dilatation, and cholangitis. 
Planning for ERCP.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar, multisequential MRI of the abdomen with MRCP was
performed at pre and post the uneventful administration of 6 mL of Gadavist
intravenous contrast.

COMPARISON:  Compared with previous MRI abdomen from ___.

FINDINGS: 

There is irregular nodular intrahepatic bile ducts (9:1) with atrophy of
segments within the left and right hepatic lobes compatible with known primary
sclerosing cholangitis; the overall appearance is similar when compared to the
prior examination. There is mild hyperenhancement of the intrahepatic bile
ducts and common bile duct which is overall similar when compared to the prior
examination and also in keeping with primary sclerosing cholangitis.  There
are no findings to suggest acute cholangitis.

There is a 5 mm filling defect within the common hepatic duct, which most
probably represents an obstructive stone (9:1).  Again noted is high
termination of the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct which may reflect
sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (3:28).

The liver demonstrates diffuse heterogeneous appearance on T2 weighted images
within the right and left lower lobe with areas of confluent fibrosis, overall
similar to previous.  The portal vein is patent.

The adrenal glands, kidneys, pancreas, appear unremarkable.  There has been
prior cholecystectomy.  There is mild splenomegaly with the spleen measuring
up to 13.8 cm.  There is no upper intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal
lymphadenopathy.

The lung bases appear unremarkable.

The bone marrow signal intensity is within normal lumen limits.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  5 mm filling defect within the common hepatic duct, which most probably
represents an obstructive stone

2.  Confluent hepatic fibrosis and irregular intrahepatic bile ducts with
hepatic atrophy in keeping with known primary sclerosing cholangitis similar
to the prior examination from ___.

3.  High termination the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct which may
reflect Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.

4.  Mild splenomegaly.

NOTIFICATION:  Findings discussed with Dr. ___ at 12:15PM on ___, 10 minutes after discovery and Dr. ___ at 11 AM on ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted for right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain before—same spot, under my ribs. It started a few days ago. I had a low-grade fever at home, around 99.6, and felt nauseous. My hepatologist started me on doxycycline, but I wasn’t getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of primary sclerosing cholangitis and past cholangitis episodes, this could be another flare. We’ll run some tests to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried it might be. I’ve had this so many times. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s treatable. We’ll start antibiotics right away to cover any infection, even though you’re not running a high fever now. We also need to check if there’s a stone blocking your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time there was a stone. Can’t they just remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll find out. You’re scheduled for an ultrasound first. If we see a stone, we may need an MRCP or ERCP to get a better look and possibly remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back. It shows a retained stone in the central intrahepatic ducts, possibly in the right hepatic duct. No bile duct dilation, which is good, but it could still be causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the same stone again? Why can’t they get it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in a tricky spot. But we’re not giving up. We’re ordering an MRCP tomorrow for a more detailed view. That’ll help us plan the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the antibiotics? You said you’d start me on something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting IV meropenem. It’s broad-spectrum and safe for you, given your allergies to sulfa and penicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I had diarrhea last time on doxycycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. For now, focus on resting. We’ll check your labs and see how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood and urine cultures came back negative—no infection in the blood. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cultures are negative, but your symptoms and history suggest cholangitis. We’re continuing meropenem because it’s likely a bile duct issue that doesn’t always show up in blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the MRCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow morning. It’ll show us the exact location of the stone and the condition of your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRCP is done. It shows a 5 mm filling defect in the common hepatic duct—likely a stone. There’s also confirmation of your PSC changes: fibrosis and irregular ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they can remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve scheduled an ERCP for tomorrow. We’ll try to remove the stone using a balloon sweep. Given it’s embedded, we may use a special scope—Spyglass—to see it directly and take biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies? Is there a cancer concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. Sometimes tissue grows over stones, and we want to make sure it’s not abnormal. But your prior tests were negative, so we’re optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will I know how it went?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is at 12 tomorrow. I’ll come by afterward to update you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the ERCP. The good news: we found an embedded stone in the common hepatic duct. We used Spyglass and biopsies to loosen it, then cleared a portion with a balloon sweep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least part of it. We got a piece out, and the duct is now draining better. The tissue over the stone showed chronic inflammation, which fits your PSC. The biopsies will be checked for IgG4 to rule out another condition, but that’s routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still improving. We’re switching from IV meropenem to oral ciprofloxacin. You’ll take it for 9 more days at home. After that, resume your rifaximin for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely by Friday. We’ll watch your labs and make sure you’re stable. Your liver enzymes are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are trending well. WBC is normal, bilirubin is down. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel better already. Less pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on cipro, ursodiol, and your other meds. We’re adding a mild laxative, senna, in case the oxycodone for pain causes constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I’ll drink more water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Fiber too—fruits and veggies. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ at the liver center in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your final labs look good. No fever, pain is minimal, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. Will I keep getting these stones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With PSC, there’s a risk, but rifaximin helps reduce flares. We’ll monitor with imaging as needed. The ERCP helped clear the blockage, which should reduce recurrence for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other conditions—thyroid, blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All stable. You’ll continue levothyroxine, lisinopril, furosemide, and omeprazole. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And depression? I’ve been feeling down with all these hospital visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re feeling that way. Keep taking your escitalopram. Please mention this at your follow-up—mental health is part of your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Take ciprofloxacin twice daily for 9 days, then restart rifaximin. Use oxycodone only if needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the senna?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you’re constipated. Drink fluids and eat fiber first. Call if you have fever, worsening pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee. Happy Birthday, by the way—I saw it on your badge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oh—thank you! That’s very kind. Take care, and I hope your next visit is just a routine check-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. I’ll see you or Dr. ___ soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll get your ERCP biopsy results and follow up. You’re doing well—keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The team will help you with discharge paperwork and getting home safely.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis and cirrhosis was admitted for recurrent right upper quadrant pain and nausea, consistent with cholangitis. She had been started on doxycycline by her hepatologist without improvement. Initial labs showed mild abnormalities, and blood and urine cultures were negative. Imaging revealed a 5 mm obstructive stone in the common hepatic duct. She underwent ERCP with Spyglass cholangioscopy, during which an embedded stone was identified and partially removed using biopsies and balloon sweeps. She was treated with IV meropenem, transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin for completion at home, and showed clinical improvement. Her chronic conditions, including hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, and depression, were managed throughout. She was discharged home with a plan to complete antibiotics, resume rifaximin, and follow up with the liver center.
